claims.text: Temperature-dependent local lattice distortions caused by thermal-expansion mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr govern the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior.
Local lattice distortions alter the elastic anisotropy of HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions promote enhanced edge-dislocation activity at elevated temperatures.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has a single-phase BCC structure.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent atomic-scale lattice distortions arising from compositional heterogeneity.
Thermal cycling under constant-strain-rate loading can be combined with in situ neutron diffraction and elastic-modulus modeling to test the hypothesis.
Cold rolling enhances lattice distortions relative to a homogenized or as-cast baseline.
Comparing homogenized and pre-deformed samples isolates the influence of lattice distortion.
Differential thermal expansion creates local elastic inhomogeneities.
Local elastic inhomogeneities modify diffraction elastic moduli.
Differential thermal expansion drives a shift toward edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity at elevated temperatures.
Elevated temperatures will increase lattice-strain heterogeneity relative to room temperature.
Elevated temperatures will alter the elastic moduli relative to room temperature.
Cold-rolled samples will show a more pronounced increase in edge-dislocation activity than baseline samples.
Cold-rolled samples will show a measurable shift between theoretical and experimental elastic moduli.
Baseline samples have minimal induced lattice distortion, relatively uniform elastic moduli, and standard room-temperature dislocation behavior.
A lack of significant differences in lattice-strain heterogeneity, elastic moduli, and dislocation character between cold-rolled and homogenized samples would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between thermal-expansion mismatch and mechanical behavior would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require identical processing histories for baseline and modified samples, but the proposed comparison deliberately gives one set a homogenized history and the other a cold-rolling history.
The as-cast state is described as having inherent lattice distortions, while the as-cast or homogenized sample is also allowed to serve as a baseline characterized by minimal induced distortion.
